https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: The carbon noose is tightening. Can Labour keep voters onside?
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
On Wednesday, a committee you’ve probably never heard of will publish the most important document you’ll never read. It will do more than any budget or industrial strategy to set the terms of trade for the economy — drawing the lines inside which politicians are left to colour.
What is this extraordinary manuscript? The UK’s seventh carbon budget, published by the Climate Change Committee (CCC), which is at the heart of the process that turns net zero from abstract aspiration into concrete fact.
Under its net zero commitment, Britain is legally obliged to have eliminated its greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Every five years, the CCC publishes an update on how we are doing — including advice to parliament on how much carbon we can emit.
The sixth carbon budget, published in 2020, called for emissions for 2033-37 to be barely a fifth of levels in the benchmark year of 1990. And the targets in the seventh, covering the years 2038-42, will be even tighter.
These targets — once adopted by government, as they inevitably are — are not just tough but binding. If ministers don’t produce convincing plans to meet them, environmental groups will sue and win — as they have repeatedly done. Of course, the government doesn’t have to go along with the CCC’s specific proposals. But the logic of carbon budgeting is that if you do less in one area or period, you have to do more in another to make the numbers add up.
• What the court ruling on North Sea oil and gas means for Scotland
On the face of it, this system makes sense. If you’re going to have net zero targets, you have to have a mechanism to deliver them — and to force the upfront investment that will (the CCC and others argue) deliver a cleaner, brighter future.
But the system has helped trap the energy debate between two poles. On one end are those who believe any sacrifice is worthwhile. The Guardian gleefully predicted, in its preview of the seventh budget, that “more action will be needed in the short and longer term, in every sector of the economy, involving changes to nearly every aspect of our lives from how we live at home to how we get around, what we work on and what we eat”.
The problem, of course, is that people don’t like being told how to live, work and get around, let alone what to eat. Which is why many of the suggestions in the sixth budget went down badly — such as ending the sale of gas boilers by 2033 or capping UK airport capacity. Even Ed Miliband, the great climate warrior, recently admitted: “I am very wary of saying that we will stop people having gas boilers at a point when we cannot guarantee that heat pumps will be cheaper for people.”
• Carbon budgets are having increasingly perverse effects
There is also something of a conflict with the government’s stated priorities. Going for growth, housebuilding, expanding Heathrow — all risk falling foul of the carbon curbs and the courts.At the other end of the spectrum, of course, are those who denounce the whole thing as a racket. Last week, citing the late Patrick Moore, Nigel Farage claimed that “sunspot activity and underwater volcanic activity will always have a bigger impact on the environment than man himself ever can”. Given that the ten most recent years are also, globally, the ten hottest since the 1880s, those volcanoes must be outdoing themselves.
Others, however, such as Kemi Badenoch, describe themselves not as climate sceptic but “net zero sceptic” — particularly since there is a ratchet built into the system. If we fall behind on our path to 2050 — as we have — then the budgets have to get tougher, and the interventions more dramatic.
The public still strongly support action on climate change, and indeed the net zero target. But that support is getting wobblier. In recent polling by Lord Ashcroft, an overwhelming majority of voters agreed — despite Miliband’s best efforts to claim otherwise — that net zero would mean higher costs for them personally. There were also sharp left-right divides on whether net zero was worth it if it meant higher costs, whether Britain should still try to lead the world, and whether our actions would meaningfully affect climate change as a whole.
• Heathrow expansion: Reeves sets out plans to speed up process
In other words, the scene is set for an ugly dynamic. The inexorable logic of the carbon budgets pushes us to make more and more sacrifices. When voters and businesses understandably balk, the targets get tougher — and the grumbling gets louder.
Already, car manufacturers are howling about the electric vehicle (EV) mandate, which forces them to make more and more EVs, whether or not anyone wants to buy them — even as the Chinese swamp the market. Stiff carbon levies contribute to sky-high energy bills for companies and consumers alike; bills that, alongside other policies, have left the chemicals industry “heading for extinction”, according to Sir Jim Ratcliffe. And then there’s the North Sea. Or rather, there was the North Sea.
Is there a better way? Well, as a nerdy free-marketeer, I’d say the best solution would be to forget all the fiddly micromanaging and set a clear carbon price across the economy, while reducing taxation elsewhere. Politicians could then raise or lower that price depending on how far we are from our targets and/or how seriously they take the matter.
But even within the current framework, we could do so much better. In particular, climate change is a global problem, and it needs global solutions. Yet our entire net zero approach is based on what happens in Britain, and Britain alone.
Counting only emissions that are produced here, rather than consumed here, means that if a steel plant shuts down, it counts as a win for our carbon budget — even if we start importing girders fresh from the dirtiest coal-powered furnace. That we devastate the oil and gas sector, only to import the same hydrocarbons from, among others, authoritarian petrostates. That we apply climate taxes to goods (or electricity) produced here, but not to competing imports.
• Government loses High Court fight over climate change plan
Similarly, the essential purpose of climate policy should be to achieve maximum decarbonisation at minimum expense. So why not give firms credit for the carbon-cutting technology they invent and export? If it is just as good for the planet, and a damn sight cheaper, to clean up a coal plant in Laos than to replace a steel furnace in Port Talbot, why not incentivise the former?
As of 2023, Britain had cut emissions by more than half the levels it pumped out in 1990 — an extraordinary and genuinely world-leading achievement. But under the current approach, we risk lashing ourselves to the carbon mast even as other countries, notably the United States, swing decisively in the other direction. A world in which net zero means fewer flights, higher bills, fewer jobs and compulsory veganism is not one voters want — nor one they’ll accept.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Shell restarts production at Penguins North Sea oil field
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: The facility, which has been shut for four years for redevelopment, could yield the equivalent of 100 million barrels of oil over the next two decades
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Shell has restarted production from the Penguins oil field in the North Sea after a four-year hiatus to install new infrastructure.
The facility, 150 miles northeast of the Shetland islands, could yield the equivalent of 100 million barrels of oil over the next two decades, Shell said, with production expected to peak at the equivalent of about 45,000 barrels of oil per day.
Penguins was discovered in 1974 and operations were started there in 2003. It used to produce oil through undersea pipes via the Brent Charlie platform, which stopped production in 2021 and is being decommissioned. From Brent Charlie, oil was piped to the Sullom Voe terminal in Shetland where it was loaded onto tankers and exported.
As part of the redevelopment Shell has installed a dedicated floating production, storage and offloading (FPSO) vessel on the Penguins field, enabling oil to be transferred directly on to tankers for export to refineries around the world. The field lies in water depth of 165 metres and the FPSO is a cylindrical shape, designed to be more efficient and to better withstand the harsh conditions in the North Sea than conventional ship-shaped FPSOs.
Penguins also produces some gas, which is piped into an existing pipeline network and goes onshore at St Fergus in Scotland where it feeds into the national grid. Shell said that Penguins would produce enough gas to heat about 700,000 UK homes a year.
It is Shell’s first new operated facility in the North Sea for more than two decades. The company is also in the process of developing the Jackdaw gas field, which it hopes will enter into production next year. However, it suffered a major setback last week when a Scottish court quashed consent for the Jackdaw project because the government and regulators had not considered the emissions that would be generated when the gas it produces is burnt.
Shell is Europe’s biggest oil and gas company and one of the biggest producers in the UK North Sea, with output equivalent to about 80,000 barrels of oil per day last year. Shell announced in December that it was combining its UK North Sea oil and gas businesses with Equinor’s to create a 50-50 joint venture that will rank as the UK’s largest independent oil and gas company.
The venture’s output will be further bolstered by its share of production from the Penguins field, which Shell operates and owns 50-50 with Neo Energy. The company said that the Penguins FPSO would have about 30 per cent lower operational emissions than Brent Charlie.
Zoë Yujnovich, Shell’s director for its integrated gas and upstream businesses, said: “Today, the UK relies on imports to meet much of its demand for oil and gas. The Penguins field is a source of the secure domestic energy production people need today, and the FPSO is a demonstration of our investment in competitive projects that create more value with less emissions.”
Shell said that although the oil from Penguins would be transported to refineries overseas, some of these refineries supplied refined fuels back to Britain.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Meet the activists: who are the most feared investors?
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
UK boards beware: the activists may have you in their sights. A combination of weak valuations, perceived poor management and underperformance compared with international peers has made our listed companies a happy hunting ground for activist investors, particularly those from the United States.
Elliott Management, the New York-based hedge fund, has been in the spotlight in recent weeks as it has built up its stake in BP, forcing the oil company’s chief executive to promise a “fundamental reset” of its strategy.
Elliott is expected to use its growing influence to demand changes that could include staple items from an activist investor’s shopping list, such as ousting the chairman, clearing out the board or even breaking up the company.
Saba Capital, another US-based hedge fund activist, has also been in the headlines for its remarkable and acrimonious campaign against UK investment trusts.
According to a recent report from Alvarez & Marsal, the consultancy firm, the UK is “the most targeted geography in Europe” by activists and fourth globally, behind the US, Japan and Canada. “On average UK corporates continue to generally underperform many of their global peers in delivering gross margins, cash generation and return on capital,” the report said.
The UK is also a relative underperformer in terms of valuations. The FTSE 100 trades on a forward price to earnings multiple of 12 times, about half what the typical American company listed on Wall Street is valued at.
That is despite Footsie companies offering, on average, a dividend yield of 3.7 per cent versus 1.2 per cent on the S&P 500, which tracks 500 of the biggest US businesses.
Activists looking for the next victory will be emboldened by memorable successes from recent years.
For example, Unilever shares are up about a third since Trian Fund Management, Nelson Peltz’s hedge fund, started building a stake in the Marmite maker back in early 2022. He subsequently pushed his way on to the group’s board and promised to “help drive Unilever’s strategy, operations, sustainability and shareholder value for the benefit of all stakeholders”.
Before that, in 2018 after months of lobbying, Sachem Head, another American hedge fund, got its way when Whitbread agreed to sell Costa Coffee to Coca-Cola for £3.9 billion.
Sachem’s argument was that there was little, if any, benefit in having Costa and Premier Inn, Whitbread’s other business, under one roof. Whitbread returned £2.5 billion of the sale proceeds to its shareholders. The timing of the sale was fortuitous, given it completed in 2019, the year before the pandemic, when Costa’s shops were shut for months on end.
Activists do not just get involved to push for the break-up of a company to try to release some hidden value. Another strategy they can pursue is known as “bumpitrage”. A textbook example is Elliott’s intervention in the $100 billion-plus acquisition of SABMiller, the FTSE 100 brewer, by Anheuser-Busch InBev, the Budweiser owner, almost a decade ago.
The complex takeover, the biggest in British corporate history, involved a two-part offer. One comprised unlisted AB InBev paper and a small amount of cash, which in theory was open to all investors. In practice, however, it was only attractive to SAB’s biggest shareholders, Altria, the tobacco company, and the Colombian Santo Domingo family, for tax reasons.
The other element was an all-cash offer, which most other investors were likely to accept because they would find it difficult to hold unlisted stock. The all-cash portion was originally worth more than the paper-and-cash deal, but sterling’s sharp fall following the June 2016 Brexit vote meant the unlisted share offer suddenly had a higher value.
This created an opening for Elliott, which built a stake in SAB, to agitate for better terms, a so-called “bump” to the price. AB InBev eventually relented by increasing its all-cash offer and the takeover ultimately went through.
There are plenty of other reasons why an activist investor might target a company: for example, to encourage a board to return surplus cash to shareholders, to push for changes in the boardroom or to demand that a buyer for the business is sought.
• BP shares jump after Elliott hedge fund builds stake
“We are looking for a company that is doing something it shouldn’t, or not doing something it should,” John Goold, chief executive of Kelso, a small activist investor based in London, explains.
“I don’t enjoy it, but I do it because I think grannies at home who are invested in these companies deserve to be treated well. It’s all about what we think is the correct thing for a company to be doing.”
Ultimately, he says, it is about assessing whether any changes, if enacted, can push up the target’s share price.
Most activists will try to hold meetings with other shareholders before building their own stake, to canvass opinions and see if there would be support for their plans.
“You need to know your legals, you need to know the Takeover Code, you need to know the stock market and in an ideal world you need to know other shareholders, because getting their backing is key,” Goold says. “If you’ve got the support of other shareholders, that increases your chances of success.”
When it goes well, it can be a lucrative game. Cevian, the Swedish investor, made €2 billion from its efforts at Volvo. Over 11 years it pushed for the truckmaker to sell off its aerospace unit and demanded cost efficiencies to boost margins.
Its turnaround ambition was ultimately delivered when Volvo appointed a new chief executive in 2016 and the share price doubled over the next 12 months. Cevian sold its stake in 2017 for €3.25 billion, which was the largest public exit ever by an activist investor.
• GSK launches £2bn share buyback and upgrades sales forecast
Activists are not always victorious, though, and that includes Elliott, one of the most respected — and feared — players in the industry. One less successful Elliott campaign was its high-profile intervention at GSK before the pharma group’s demerger of Haleon, its consumer healthcare business, in 2022.
Elliott criticised years of “severe” underperformance, agitated for GSK to instead consider a potential sale of Haleon and questioned the continued leadership of Dame Emma Walmsley, the group chief executive, after the break-up.
In the event, the London-based group — supported by large institutional shareholders, Sir Jonathan Symonds, GSK’s chairman, and the government — went on to list Haleon as a separate FTSE 100 company, in the biggest strategic move since its formation in 2000. Walmsley, 55, remains in post.
Given his successes at Unilever, as well as Heinz, Peltz, 82, is used to getting his own way. After amassing a near-$4 billion stake in Disney in early 2024, the American billionaire investor called for two seats on the board, including one for himself, in a push to “restore the magic” at the company. He argued that it had “lost its way over the past decade”, which had cost shareholders billions of dollars.
The attack came less than two months after Bob Iger was reappointed to the top job at Disney after the ousting of Bob Chapek. The activist move effectively called into question Iger’s ability to turn the 102-year-old company around.
However, Peltz was defeated by a wide margin, with all 12 board nominees being elected at the company’s annual meeting last year, ending what was one of the most costly boardroom battles in history. Peltz sold his entire stake just two months after the proxy defeat.
A public and often acrimonious campaign isn’t always necessary for an activist to achieve their goals. According to Alvarez & Marsal, activists are increasingly looking to challenge boards via private discussions rather than public campaigns. However, the implied threat of the latter is always there. As the consultancy firm puts it in its report, “investors may speak softly but they often carry a big stick”.
• FirstGroup battles to stay on track after rail renationalisation
Even once enacted, activists’ plans are no sure thing. FirstGroup, the train operator, was forced to sell its large US businesses in 2021 after a series of investor attacks, including from Robert Tchenguiz and Coast Capital. Shareholders received £500 million from the sale but the impact, which included the departure of the chief executive, has left FirstGroup solely dependent on the UK market. That looks like a misstep now that Labour has vowed to return the railways to public ownership within five years.
Such failures are unlikely to deter activists, who have been battle-hardened by repeated clashes with boards. The expectation is that, given its lowly stock market valuations relative to others, London will continue to attract more than its fair share of investors who want to shake things up to unlock value.
“There should be more activism because [regular] investors just don’t think like this, they allow the status quo,” said one activist, who requested anonymity. “[Boards] usually don’t like being told what to do, but we are genuinely trying to help.”
Diageo may be prime target for a dose of activist refreshment. The FTSE 100 drinks giant certainly ticks boxes that normally attract such investors: a well-known consumer name that is underperforming despite owning famous brands such as Guinness and Johnnie Walker. There are question marks over management and the prospect of value-creating spin-offs.
A Bloomberg report last month that Diageo would consider a sale of Guinness, the star performer in its portfolio and thought to be worth about $10 billion, was swiftly denied. Yet a sale would be one way to release significant value for a business whose share price has been languishing around a five-year low.
The question of how to revive the fortunes of ITV has persisted through much of the seven-year tenure of Carolyn McCall, the broadcaster’s chief executive. The FTSE 250 constituent has not yet attracted the attention of activist investors, but with the share price languishing at about 75p, less than half its value at the start of 2018, it could be ripe for agitation.
A potential carve-out of the ITV Studios business from the traditional ads-based business has frequently been mooted as a way of unlocking value from the business. With RedBird IMI, the Abu Dhabi-backed fund, in early-stage talks to merge All3Media, its production arm, with ITV Studios, there is the possibility that ITV will undertake a reshaping of its own accord.
Hammerson, the shopping centre landlord, is no stranger to activist investors, although there isn’t one on the shareholder register at the moment. Rita-Rose Gagné has tidied up the portfolio and the balance sheet over the past four years, but that progress is not completely evident in the share price. Might an activist demand the company find a buyer to try to get a more appropriate valuation of the business?
Two of its ten remaining malls are in France, which look out of place in a UK property company. It is possible that someone may call for those to be sold and the proceeds reinvested in development opportunities around its UK sites.
The share price at Legal & General is at exactly the same level as in January last year, when the former Santander banker António Simões arrived to add some zing to the business. Neither the strategic review of last July nor the new alliance unveiled last week with Meiji Yasuda, the Japanese insurer, have yet triggered any re-rating of the shares. The promise of £5 billion of dividends and buybacks over three years will keep some shareholders happy, but some look at the pin-up of the sector, Aviva, and wonder whether a bit of activist chivvying couldn’t do the same for L&G.
Smiths Group,the last industrial conglomerate on the London market, has already acted following pressure from investors. In January it announced plans to sell or demerge two of its four core divisions and return much of the proceeds to shareholders, sending its shares up 11 per cent. It will now focus on industrial technologies.
The break-up plan is said to have been in the works since Roland Carter took over as chief executive last March, although there was no indication in its response to an open letter demanding change from the New York activists Engine Capital. It emerged that Elliott Management had also built a stake in the business before the announcement.
